papers.title: Real-time Bayesian inference at extreme scale: A digital twin for tsunami early warning applied to the Cascadia subduction zone
papers.field: Computational geophysics; Bayesian inverse problems; real-time tsunami forecasting
papers.summary: The authors combine seafloor-pressure observations with a three-dimensional acoustic-gravity model to infer earthquake-driven seafloor motion and predict coastal wave heights with uncertainty. Shift invariance and block-Toeplitz algorithms move expensive PDE solves into one-time offline preparation. The resulting online inference takes less than 0.2 seconds on 512 A100 GPUs for a synthetic Cascadia scenario; the offline wave solver separately scales to 55.5 trillion degrees of freedom on El Capitan.

machine_configurations.facility: Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL)
machine_configurations.configuration: As described in this manuscript: HPE Cray EX, 11,136 nodes, four AMD Instinct MI300A APUs per node. Each APU integrates 24 Zen4 CPU cores, a CDNA3 GPU and 128 GB HBM3. HPE Slingshot-200 dragonfly interconnect. Scaling experiments used 85-10,880 nodes / 340-43,520 APUs (called GPUs in the paper).
machine_configurations.location: PDF pp. 7-9, section VI.A, Table II, Fig. 5.

machine_configurations.facility: Swiss National Supercomputing Centre (CSCS)
machine_configurations.configuration: As described in this manuscript: HPE Cray EX, 2,688 nodes, four NVIDIA GH200 superchips per node; each has a 72-core Grace CPU and H100 GPU with 96 GB HBM3. Slingshot-11 dragonfly interconnect. Scaling run: 36-2,304 nodes / 144-9,216 GPUs.
machine_configurations.location: PDF pp. 7-9, section VI.A, Table II, Fig. 5.

measurements.precision: Double precision
measurements.scope: Online Phase 4 Bayesian parameter inference: strict upper bound (<0.2 s), excluding offline preparation
measurements.scale: 128 Perlmutter nodes / 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs; 2,416,530 spatial parameter points x 420 temporal steps (~1.015 billion parameters), 252,000 synthetic noisy observations from 600 hypothesized sensors, and 21 forecast locations.
measurements.location: PDF p. 10, section VII.C and Table III (Phase 4); parameter discretization on p. 7.
measurements.measurement_method: Wall time measured using omp_get_wtime after GPU synchronization and MPI_Barrier (section VI.D, p. 8).
measurements.note: The source reports less than 0.2 s, not an exact 0.2 s value. Phase 1 alone requires 621 independent PDE solutions totaling about 538 hours on 512 GPUs; later offline phases also precede the online result. Table III separately lists QoI-only prediction at <1 ms on one GPU. Synthetic noisy data, not an operational sensor-to-alert deployment benchmark.

measurements.precision: Double precision
measurements.scope: Weak parallel efficiency of the offline acoustic-gravity PDE solver
measurements.scale: 85 to 10,880 nodes / 340 to 43,520 AMD MI300A GPUs; 128-fold increase in GPUs and problem size; largest problem >55.5 trillion DOF (~1.28 billion DOF/APU), using 4.8 PB of memory.
measurements.location: PDF pp. 8-9, section VII.A, Table II and Fig. 5 (left).
measurements.measurement_method: Runtime per RK4 step averaged over ten consecutive time steps (40 operator applications), after discarding the initial ten steps. POSIX wall clocks called after device synchronization and MPI_Barrier (p. 8, section VI.C).
measurements.note: This is an offline-solver scaling efficiency, not the speed or GPU count of the <0.2 s online inference. Table II separates weak-scaling mesh elements from strong-scaling elements per GPU. The distinct strong-scaling test fixes 434 billion DOF and reports 100.9x speedup / 79% efficiency.

measurements.precision: Double precision
measurements.scope: FFT-based Hessian matrix-vector product after precomputing the parameter-to-observation map
measurements.scale: 128 Perlmutter nodes / 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs; 2,416,530 spatial parameter points x 420 temporal steps (~1.015 billion parameters), 252,000 synthetic noisy observations from 600 hypothesized sensors, and 21 forecast locations.
measurements.location: PDF p. 10, section VII.C; Table III form-K row gives 24 ms per matvec.
measurements.measurement_method: Wall timings use omp_get_wtime after device synchronization and MPI_Barrier; vendor FFT/BLAS libraries (section VI.D, p. 8).
measurements.note: Reported as an exact block-Toeplitz Hessian application, without an approximation. The comparison is 104 minutes for a forward/adjoint PDE pair on the same 512 A100 GPUs versus 0.024 s after offline precomputation, yielding the paper's 260,000x speedup. This is not a whole workflow runtime.

notes: Audit uses arXiv v2 dated 2025-08-28; v1 was submitted 2025-04-23. The PDF is an author manuscript, not asserted identical to the final ACM proceedings PDF. The registry confirms the associated SC25 DOI/booktitle.
Title capitalization follows the reviewed PDF rather than the title-cased conference program. Ordered eight-author byline was visually verified across its three rows.

All computations are explicitly double precision (section VI, p. 7). The authors prioritize time-to-solution / DOF throughput over maximizing FLOP/s; no whole-machine FLOP/s is inferred from the scaling result.
Reported hardware inventory is manuscript-specific and is not updated to a current machine inventory.
The abstract rounds online inference to 0.2 s, whereas Table III and section VII.C give <0.2 s. The strict bound is retained in the detailed measurement.
No conference presentation update or award-final numerical score was checked.

Award status is verified separately from ACM's own press release distributed through EurekAlert, explicitly identified as issued by the Association for Computing Machinery. Award recognition does not establish any numerical result as a conference-updated or award-final score.

papers.title: Ab-initio Quantum Transport with the GW Approximation, 42,240 Atoms, and Sustained Exascale Performance
papers.field: Quantum transport; semiconductor nanodevices; many-body electronic-structure computation
papers.summary: QuaTrEx combines non-equilibrium Green's functions with self-consistent GW electron-interaction calculations to model silicon nanoribbon transistors at experimentally relevant dimensions. A spatial decomposition and recursive Green's-function solver distribute large devices over accelerator ranks. A 42,240-atom case sustains 1,146.037 Pflop/s in FP64 on Frontier, while Alps reaches 342.637 Pflop/s for 46,464 atoms. These are per-iteration application measurements excluding I/O.

machine_configurations.configuration: As described in this manuscript: 9,604 HPE Cray EX235a nodes, each with one 64-core AMD EPYC Trento CPU and four AMD Instinct MI250X GPU packages. Each MI250X comprises two graphics compute dies (GCDs), each with 64 GB HBM; one MPI rank per GCD. Near-full benchmark uses 9,400 nodes = 37,600 MI250X packages = 75,200 GCDs/ranks. Slingshot network and intranode Infinity Fabric.

papers.title: Democratizing AI: Open-source Scalable LLM Training on GPU-based Supercomputers
papers.field: Distributed machine learning; large language model training
papers.summary: AxoNN combines four dimensions of model and data parallelism to train large transformer models across NVIDIA and AMD supercomputers. Kernel tuning, communication overlap and a performance model reduce training costs while allowing models too large for one accelerator. The paper benchmarks weak scaling on three systems, predicts longer training times from short iteration measurements, and uses the framework to study model memorization and a mitigation through fine-tuning.

papers.title: Breaking the Molecular Dynamics Timescale Barrier Using a Wafer-Scale System
papers.field: Computational materials science; classical molecular dynamics
papers.summary: This work maps each simulated atom to a processor core on a Cerebras wafer-scale engine and uses local dataflow communication to accelerate Embedded Atom Method molecular dynamics. The approach targets the time horizon of a fixed-size simulation, which is limited by communication latency on conventional CPU/GPU clusters. Uniform copper, tungsten and tantalum crystals and a grain-boundary case demonstrate the method; the audited May 2024 version reports measured loop rates for roughly 802,000 atoms and separately models future optimizations and multi-wafer extensions.

notes: Audited source is a complete 13-page author manuscript served by the PETSc-FUN3D project at Argonne, with the exact title and ordered initials above. The PDF has no abstract heading; the English summary here is editorial and is not a reproduced abstract. The author project’s publication list identifies this work as the SC99 paper and links its ICASE 2000-2 report relationship.

The source has no visible issue/revision date or authenticated version history. PDF metadata CreationDate is D:19990925114528, without a timezone; this supports identification of the retrieved file but is not promoted to source_revision_date or measurement_date. The name bell.pdf is not treated as proof of final conference status.

Exact manuscript byline is retained in initials. The author publication list separately expands the names as Kyle Anderson, William D. Gropp, Dinesh K. Kaushik, David E. Keyes and Barry F. Smith; those forms must remain searchable without replacing the verified PDF byline.

Large-scale tests in this manuscript concern the Euler subset. FUN3D also supports Navier-Stokes and a Spalart–Allmaras turbulence model, but the text describes that work on more modest problems and as future scale-up; the reported large-machine headline is not mislabeled as a turbulent Navier-Stokes production run.

The nonlinear method uses pseudo-transient continuation, inexact Newton iteration, a matrix-free Krylov method and an additive Schwarz preconditioner derived from a lower-order, sparser discretization. PETSc provides distributed objects and MPI communication, and MeTiS partitions the mesh. Data interlacing, structural blocking, vertex/edge reordering and communication overlap improve data reuse and parallel execution.

Four selected headline observations are retained, two native metrics for each of two machines. This first pass does not transcribe every point of the scaling figures or every kernel/flow-regime table entry. Tables 1-2 use a separate 357,900-vertex mesh, and Figure 2 uses 22,677 vertices with four unknowns per vertex.

Figure 2 machine-peak and STREAM Triad bars are bounds/comparators for coarse sequential tests. The 235 Mflop/s instruction-scheduling estimate and 209 Mflop/s hardware-counter result in Section 3.2 concern the SGI flux kernel. The historical NWT 111 Gflop/s claim in the conclusion is an attributed prior-work comparison. None is added as a FUN3D large-mesh solver measurement.

ASCI Red topology labels need care: the overview and Section 5.2 explicitly say 2,048 dual-processor nodes, while Section 5’s introduction and Figure 4 caption use processors. The selected scale follows the explicit dual-node description, preserves the runtime-mode distinction and does not infer that both CPUs execute the complete solver.

A separately saved NASA/CR-2000-210080 / ICASE 2000-2 report has a January 2000 cover and reports 3,072 dual-processor nodes, 227 Gflop/s and 15 microseconds per degree of freedom. Only its cover, byline/abstract and overview (PDF pp. 1-3) were checked for this version comparison. Those values are not substituted into the 156 Gflop/s manuscript or added to the selected fully audited observations.

Neither the partial January 2000 variant check nor the project publication-list award wording establishes a conference-day final score. Measurement calendar dates and floating-point formats remain unestablished; existing independently sourced award metadata must be preserved during integration.
This is one audited 1999 candidate manuscript, not an assertion that the annual candidate roster or the year’s full-text work is complete.

papers.title: Large Scale Simulation of Suspensions with PVM
papers.field: Suspension rheology and parallel boundary-element simulation
papers.summary: The study models how particles alter a suspension’s resistance to falling and rotating test spheres. A completed double-layer boundary-element formulation avoids storing a large dense system, while asynchronous particle-wise updates distribute the work through PVM. Calculations on a shared AlphaStation farm compare sedimentation and rotational responses across concentrations. The performance analysis uses extrapolated serial-equivalent work and keeps wall-clock throughput separate from CPU-time throughput.

machine_configurations.name: DEC AlphaStation 500/266 workstation farm
machine_configurations.facility: Workstation farm described by the University of Sydney authors; the machine-description section does not explicitly name a room or facility.
machine_configurations.configuration: 28 DEC AlphaStation 500/266 workstations with DEC AXP 21164 processors linked by 100-Mbit/s Fast Ethernet. Listed configuration is 128 Mbytes of memory and a 4-Gbyte disk per workstation; footnote 2 states that two workstations instead have 512 Mbytes. PVM handles message passing; a coordinating task farms particle-surface solves to workers and broadcasts updated solutions. Runs took place under normal time-sharing load.
machine_configurations.location: HTML Workstation Farm / Computer Description and Cost Estimation; Footnotes 1–2; derived PDF pp. 5 and 9

research.problem: Compute suspension flow resistance in creeping-flow Stokes problems, using a falling or rotating test sphere inside a concentrated suspension; the authors explicitly distinguish this configuration-dependent resistance from an intrinsic shear viscosity.
research.algorithm: Completed Double Layer Boundary Element Method (CDLBEM); particle-surface domain decomposition with block-Jacobi-like updates and relaxation 0.5; asynchronous updates of the potential when a worker finishes; PVM task farming. Each particle/container surface has 96 or 150 nine-node quadrilateral elements, Gaussian quadrature, and stated relative convergence thresholds of 1e-3 for the potential and velocity changes.
research.scientific_result: The calculated sedimentation response rises more sharply with particle concentration and varies more across configurations than the rotational response. The paper compares values with Thomas’ experimental bounds and empirical relations, and illustrates improved convergence from asynchronous updating for a 35% volume-fraction configuration.
research.location: HTML Formulation / Problem Description, CDLBEM and Domain Decomposition, Numerical Scheme; Results / Suspension Viscosities; derived PDF pp. 2–6

papers.title: N-body Simulation of Galaxy Formation on GRAPE-4 Special-Purpose Computer
papers.field: Computational astrophysics; high-resolution gravitational N-body simulation of galaxy formation
papers.summary: Fukushige and Makino follow the collapse of a cold-dark-matter density peak with direct gravitational interactions, fourth-order Hermite integration and individual hierarchical timesteps. GRAPE-4 pipelines calculate gravitational forces and their time derivatives while a DEC host integrates particle orbits. The calculation uses 786,400 particles to resolve the developing galaxy more finely; the audited author version reports a whole-run average application rate and a separate cost-per-performance estimate.

machine_configurations.name: GRAPE-4
machine_configurations.facility: University of Tokyo (authors’ affiliation; installation room not specified).
machine_configurations.configuration: The audited run uses three of the system’s four clusters. Each active cluster has a host-interface board, control board and nine processor boards. Each processor board has one PROMETHEUS predictor chip, particle-data memory and 48 physical HARP chips, with 47 used for calculation. There are 1,269 active HARP pipelines at 32 MHz. Each pipeline performs the author-counted 49 floating-point operations in three cycles. The paper’s 663 Gflops is theoretical peak, kept separate from the 332 Gflops run average.

papers.title: 50 GFlops Molecular Dynamics on the Connection Machine 5
papers.field: Short-range molecular dynamics and atomistic materials simulation
papers.summary: SPaSM makes large atomistic materials simulations practical by dividing space into processor domains and smaller interaction cells. It exchanges particle data across domain boundaries, evaluates short-range forces on the CM-5 vector units, and caches cells in vector-accessible memory. The study compares interaction cutoffs and scaling, showing why a faster particle update can have a lower FLOP rate, and illustrates the method with an impact simulation.

machine_configurations.name: Connection Machine CM-5
machine_configurations.facility: The authors are affiliated with the Theoretical Division and Advanced Computing Laboratory, Los Alamos National Laboratory. The performance section identifies CM-5 partitions but does not individually identify a facility for every timing.
machine_configurations.configuration: Runs use 32–1,024 processing nodes, plus a 4-node scaling example. Each node has a SPARC processor, four vector units at a stated peak of 32 Mflops each, and four 8-Mbyte memory banks (32 Mbytes per node). Node memory is divided into SPARC and parallel-memory allocations. ANSI C calls CMMD explicitly; an approximately 60-line CDPEAC assembly kernel evaluates forces. The paper states 128 GFlops theoretical peak for a 1,024-node machine.
machine_configurations.location: Derived PDF pp. 2–4, sections 2–4; p. 6, section 5

research.problem: Integrate Newtonian dynamics for very large 3-D systems of particles with short-range interactions, aimed at defects, fracture and impact in materials.
research.workload: Lennard-Jones 6-12 pair potential with interaction cutoffs of 5 sigma and 2.5 sigma; all calculations double precision. The timing setup begins with a cubic lattice chosen to rearrange into an fcc configuration, so particles migrate across processors.
research.algorithm: Geometric domain decomposition; each processing node subdivides its region into cells just larger than the cutoff. An interaction path visits neighboring cells, exploiting Newton’s third law; CMMD exchanges cell data and asynchronously redistributes moved particles. Four vector units evaluate blocks of interactions. A FIFO cache of cells in parallel memory reduces repeated transfers from SPARC memory.
research.location: Derived PDF pp. 1–5; impact example pp. 6–8

measurements.location: Derived PDF p. 6, Table 1 and section 5; precision p. 2; counting/timing method p. 5

Computation includes forces and numerical integration; communication includes message passing for force evaluation and particle redistribution. I/O and initialization inclusion are not specified.
